Q: Does jit compiler parallelize list comprehension with independent statements in `jax` A:

Outside of a jit context, list comprehensions will be executed eagerly, with each execution dispatching asynchronously (see Asynchronous Dispatch for details). This means that Python does not have to wait for device-side computations to complete before moving on to dispatch the next operation in the loop. When the operations are expensive and the device-side computation takes longer than the Python dispatch time, this can be important, and allow for some degree of parallelization by the backend.

Another important piece here is JIT compilation. jnp.cumsum itself is JIT-compiled by default (see the source), and so each iteration of the function on a different shape or dtype will result in a recompilation, which slows down the dispatch speed of your code even further.

what would be best practice to optimize execution time in such scenario?

The best thing you could do here to improve the speed of code like this would be to pad the arrays to a common shape, stack them into a single array, and use jax.vmap to vectorize the operation over those arrays. That looks pretty doable in the simple example in your question, but depending on the actual operation and the distribution of array sizes you're working with, it may not be feasible.

Q: How can I loop over directories in Linux? A:

TL;DR:

(cd /tmp; for d in */; do echo "${d%/}"; done)

Explanation

There isn’t any need to use external programs. You need a shell globbing pattern. To avoid the need of removing folder /tmp afterward, I'm running it in a subshell, which may or not be suitable for your purposes.

Shell globbing patterns in a nutshell:

  • * Match any nonempty string any number of times.
  • ? Match exactly one character.
  • [...] Matches with a character from between the brackets. You can also specify ranges ([a-z], [A-F0-9], etc.) or classes ([:digit:], [:alpha:], etc.).
  • [^...] Match one of the characters not between the braces.

* If no file names match the pattern, the shell will return the pattern unchanged. Any character or string that is not one of the above represents itself.

Consequently, the pattern */ will match any file name that ends with a /. A trailing / in a file name unambiguously identifies a directory.

The last bit is removing the trailing slash, which is achieved with the variable substitution ${var%PATTERN}, which removes the shortest matching pattern from the end of the string contained in var, and where PATTERN is any valid globbing pattern. So we write ${d%/}, meaning we want to remove the trailing slash from the string represented by d.

Q: Merging two A5 pages into a singe A4 page (without using Pdfnup) A:

Don't overengineer this problem. When printing A5, just scale the print to 141%, which makes your pages match A4. Then print two pages on one, and you are done.
